**On Keeping Something Alive**

There's a jar of sourdough starter in a kitchen somewhere that has been fed flour and water every day for over a century. The yeasts and bacteria in it today are not the originals, of course. They're descendants, countless generations removed. Yet people speak of it as the same starter, passed from grandmother to granddaughter like a quilt or a recipe card stained with butter.

I find this quietly astonishing. A starter is less an object than a practice. It persists only because someone keeps showing up. Skip too many feedings and it sours into gray liquid and surrender. Tend it and it rises, bubbling, smelling faintly of apples and vinegar, ready to make bread that tastes of a particular place and a particular lineage of care.

Many of the things we value most work this way. Languages survive because people keep speaking them to children. Friendships last because someone sends the text, makes the call, remembers the birthday. Even memory is less a filing cabinet than a starter, reconstructed each time we reach for it, subtly altered, kept alive by use.

We tend to imagine permanence as something carved in stone. But stone erodes. What actually lasts is often soft, fragile, and dependent on attention: a song, a ritual, a jar of flour paste on a windowsill.

There's a lesson in that, I think. Continuity isn't something we possess. It's something we do, daily, with our hands, and then pass along, hoping someone else will keep feeding it.
